o: Given [0, n−1] and a list of covered intervals (possibly overlapping, n up to 10⁹), output the maximal uncovered gaps sorted by start. Marking cells individually is impossible at n = 10⁹, so we work purely with interval arithmetic: sort by start, sweep maintaining the furthest covered end, and emit a gap whenever the next interval starts beyond it. Example 1: covers [3,5],[7,8] → gaps [0,2],[6,6],[9,9].
k: Never materialize cells — sort intervals and sweep.
cur = one past the furthest covered end so far; a gap exists when l > cur.
Merge overlaps implicitly via cur = max(cur, r + 1).

a.i: Sort ranges by start. Keep cur, the first uncovered index not yet known to be covered. For each interval [l, r]: if l > cur, the gap [cur, l−1] is uncovered; then extend cur to max(cur, r+1). After the sweep, if cur ≤ n−1, emit the final gap [cur, n−1]. Overlapping and duplicate intervals are absorbed naturally.
s: cur = 0; for each [l, r]: if l > cur push [cur, l−1]; cur = max(cur, r + 1).
a.t: O(m log m) — sorting dominates (m = ranges.length up to 10⁶)
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond the output (ignoring sort space)

w: Classic interval-cover sweep; the same pattern solves calendar-merging and 'missing ranges' problems. Pitfalls: empty ranges list (whole [0, n−1] uncovered), fully covered input (empty output), and using cur as an exclusive end consistently. Follow-up: stream the ranges unsorted (need a different structure, e.g., a sorted container or union-find on compressed coordinates).
